exampleAnswers.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.text: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sin(2x)$ at the point where $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}\right).$
question.explanation:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ is given by $f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8} \right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = 2x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos u \qquad \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d} y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=(\cos u) \cdot (2)\\[5pt] &=2 \cos (2x). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ we find

\[ \eqalign{ f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) &=2 \cos \left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{8} \right)\\[5pt] &= 2 \cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \\[5pt] &=\sqrt 2\,. } \]

Therefore, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x =\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ is $\sqrt 2.$

example.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = x^2 +2x - 1. \]

Differentiating gives \[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2x+2. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\cos u \cdot (2x+2)\\[5pt] &=(2x+2)\cos u\\[5pt] &= (2x+2)\cos \left(x^2+2x-1 \right). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

\begin{align} f'(0) & =(2\cdot 0+2)\cos(0^2+2\cdot 0-1)\\[3pt] & =2\cos(-1)\\[3pt] &= 2\cos1 \end{align}

Therefore, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is $2\cos 1.$

question.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \cot (2\pi-3x)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac \pi 2,0\right).$
question.explanation:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = \dfrac \pi 2$ is given by $f'\left(\dfrac \pi 2\right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \cot{u}, \qquad u = 2\pi-3x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -\csc^2 u \qquad \text{and} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} y' &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\left(-\csc^2 u \right) \cdot (-3)\\[5pt] &=3\csc^2(2\pi-3x). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac {\pi}2,$ we find

\begin{align} m=f'\left(\dfrac \pi 2 \right)& =3\csc^2 \left(2\pi-\dfrac {3\pi} 2\right)\\[5pt] & =3\csc^2 \left(\dfrac \pi 2\right)\\[5pt] & =3\cdot 1^2\\[5pt] & = 3. \end{align}

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $\left(\dfrac \pi 2,0\right) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\[5pt] y-0 &= 3\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\\[5pt] y &= 3x-\dfrac{3\pi}{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.text: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\cot(2x)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8},1\right).$
question.explanation:
First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{8}$ is given by $f'\left( \dfrac{\pi}{8} \right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \cot{u}, \qquad u = 2x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = -\csc^2 u \qquad \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=-\csc^2 u \cdot \left(2\right)\\[5pt] &=-2 \csc^2 (2x). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$, we find \[ \eqalign{ f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) &=-2 \csc^2 \left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{8} \right) \\[5pt] &=-2 \csc^2 \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)\\[5pt] &=-2 \cdot \left( \sqrt 2 \right)^2\\[5pt] &=-4 \,. } \]

Therefore, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{8}$ is $-4.$

exampleAnswers.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express

\[ f(x) = 9(\sin{x})^2. \]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

\[ f = 9u^2, \qquad u=\sin x. \]

Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 18u \qquad \style{font-family:inherit;}{\text{and}} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=18u\cdot \cos{x}\\[5pt] &=18\sin{x}\cos{x}. \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express

\[ f(x) = 3(\cos{x})^{2}. \]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

\[ f = 3u^{2}, \qquad u=\cos{x}. \]

Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = 6u, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=6u\cdot (-\sin{x})\\[5pt] &=6(\cos{x})(-\sin{x})\\[5pt] &=-6\cos{x}\sin{x}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \cos{x}. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\cos u \cdot (-\sin x)\\[5pt] &=-\sin x \cos \left(\cos x \right) . \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \sec{x}. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = \sec{x}\tan {x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\cos u \cdot (\sec{x}\tan {x})\\[5pt] &=\sec{x}\tan {x} \cos \left(\sec x \right) . \end{align*}

example.title: Differentiating a Composition of Trigonometric Functions Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sec(u), \qquad u = \csc(x). \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \sec{(u)}\tan{(u)}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = -\csc{x}\cot{x}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= \sec{(u)}\tan{(u)} \cdot (-\csc{x}\cot{x})\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\csc{x}\cot{x}} \cdot \sec \left(\csc(x) \right) \cdot \tan \left(\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\csc(x)} \right). \end{align*}
